arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (el registro de decisiones). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:16370.texto: With its low horizon line, monochrome palette, and efficient paint handling, this panel is characteristic of early river landscapes by Jan van Goyen. In a society that provided a broad market for art, Van Goyen executed both small- and large-scale paintings of waterways, with varying levels of detail, to appeal to buyers at the lower and higher ends of the market. Such views of Dutch canals, moody skies, and seafaring activities appealed to collectors in the young republic, which prided itself on its maritime prowess.
aic:16370.title: Fishing Boats off an Estuary

aic:39691.texto:
Emil Carlsen combined naturalism with a bright, light-filled palette, creating a seascape that harmonizes academic painting and Impressionism. Blue sky and white clouds fill much of the canvas. The scene portrays a leisurely moment: two figures rest in the sand and look out at the rolling waves while a woman with a parasol walks along the water’s edge. Seaside tourism in New England—a subject portrayed here by Carlsen and, more famously, by Winslow Homer (on view nearby)—increased in popularity during the late 19th century, offering a respite from growing industrialism.
Trained in architecture in Copenhagen, Carlsen immigrated in 1872 to Chicago, shifting his focus to painting. After further study in Paris, he relocated to Boston in 1876, the year he executed this work.
aic:39691.title: Nantasket Beach

aic:495.texto: The Dutch Republic’s pride in its successful maritime endeavors like fishing, shipbuilding, and foreign trade contributed to the great popularity of marine paintings like this one. Such coastal scenes were one of the most popular landscape genres on the market. Here, the fishing vessels used to catch herring, called herring busses, float atop a glassy sea that stretches to meet the low horizon, disappearing into the expansive sky full of billowing clouds. Atop the ships’ tall masts, Dutch flags flutter in the wind.
aic:495.title: Coast Scene

aic:81535.texto: Although boldly brushed and almost calligraphic in form, the vessels in this composition remain identifiable as specific types. To the right of center, a side-wheel packet steamer heads up the English Channel, leaving slower sailing boats in its wake. This is one of Édouard Manet’s earliest paintings of the sea, a subject to which he returned repeatedly. He painted it in Paris along with two or three other works based on sketches he made on a vacation with his family in the northern French port of Boulogne-sur-Mer.
aic:81535.title: Sea View, Calm Weather (Vue de mer, temps calme)

aic:81535.texto: The artist; probably sold to Louis Gauthier-Lathuille, Paris, 1881, for 1,000 francs [per transcript in Leenhoff, c. 1910, p. 80]; sold to Durand-Ruel, Paris, February 20, 1900, for 20,000 francs [per Durand-Ruel, Paris, stock book (no. 5699, as La Rade de Boulogne)]; transferred from Durand-Ruel, Paris, to Durand-Ruel, New York, December 1900 [this and the following per Durand-Ruel, Paris, stock book (no. 2428, as Marine, la Rade de Boulogne)]; sold to Edward Fullerton Milliken, New York, December 31, 1900, for $10,000; sold, American Art Galleries, New York, February 14, 1902, lot 17, to Knoedler and Co., New York, as agent for Mrs. Bertha Potter Palmer (d. 1918), for $7,050; by descent in the Palmer family; given to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1922.

cma:153388.texto: In 1873, Boudin made his first visit to the important port city of Bordeaux as a guest of the resident art collector Arthur Bourges. Between 1874 and 1876, Boudin made paintings of the city's harbor and docks. This was an especially stimulating time in Boudin's career, as he was invited to exhibit in 1874 with the newly-founded Société anonyme des artistes, soon to be known as the Impressionists. As in many of his views, Boudin concentrated here on the quais or working docks where goods were loaded and unloaded and sailors left in small dinghies for the larger vessels on which they worked. The low horizon line relegates much of the canvas to pure sky, but the soaring vertical and diagonal forms of the masts complement this horizontal thrust and open space. Many contemporaries greatly admired Boudin's ability to paint skies. Here, one can see the way in which he brushed on a tan color, then went over it, probably while it was still wet, with a thin but opaque application of white, to create a fresh, airy quality. For the darker areas representing water, Boudin laid in an olive-green tone.
cma:153388.title: View of Bordeaux, from the Quai des Chartrons

cma:153388.texto: Pentimenti, the visible trace of earlier painting, appears among the diagonal rigging of the small ship at the left, indicating that the artist did not thoroughly work out his composition before beginning his picture and slightly changed the position of these lines while painting.
cma:153388.title: View of Bordeaux, from the Quai des Chartrons

La obra combina naturalismo con una paleta luminosa y llena de luz, mostrando un momento de ocio junto al mar con figuras descansando y paseando.

Por eso la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica y lo que rige es **escritura única** (la escritura única del plan). lo que no entra en la identidad del plan: `α`, N, la fusión y el `variante_id` **no** son ingredientes. la versión del prompt como ingrediente del plan: el prompt **+ su versión**, el modelo y el muestreo **sí**.
plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

4. **View of Bordeaux, from the Quai des Chartrons**
   Eugène Boudin · 1874 · oil on fabric
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1986.73

   La pintura se enfoca en los muelles y el puerto de Burdeos, con un horizonte bajo que deja mucho espacio al cielo, pintado con una calidad fresca y aireada. [1]
   El uso de colores claros y la representación de un cielo amplio y aireado contribuyen a una sensación de tranquilidad en la escena.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “In 1873, Boudin made his first visit to the important port city of Bordeaux as a guest of the resident art collector Arthur Bourges. Between 1874 and 1876, Boudin made paintings of the city's harbor and docks. This was an especially stimulating time in Boudin's career, as he was invited to exhibit in 1874 with the newly-founded Société anonyme des artistes, soon to be known as the Impressionists. As in many of his views, Boudin concentrated here on the quais or working docks where goods were loaded and unloaded and sailors left in small dinghies for the larger vessels on which they worked. The low horizon line relegates much of the canvas to pure sky, but the soaring vertical and diagonal forms of the masts complement this horizontal thrust and open space. Many contemporaries greatly admired Boudin's ability to paint skies. Here, one can see the way in which he brushed on a tan color, then went over it, probably while it was still wet, with a thin but opaque application of white, to create a fresh, airy quality. For the darker areas representing water, Boudin laid in an olive-green tone.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1986.73 · CC0 1.0

5. **Nantasket Beach**
   Emil Carlsen · 1876 · Oil on canvas · Impressionism
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/39691

   La obra combina naturalismo con una paleta luminosa y llena de luz, mostrando un momento de ocio junto al mar con figuras descansando y paseando. [1]
   La escena transmite una atmósfera tranquila y relajada, con un cielo azul y nubes blancas que llenan gran parte del lienzo.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Emil Carlsen combined naturalism with a bright, light-filled palette, creating a seascape that harmonizes academic painting and Impressionism. Blue sky and white clouds fill much of the canvas. The scene portrays a leisurely moment: two figures rest in the sand and look out at the rolling waves while a woman with a parasol walks along the water’s edge. Seaside tourism in New England—a subject portrayed here by Carlsen and, more famously, by Winslow Homer (on view nearby)—increased in popularity during the late 19th century, offering a respite from growing industrialism.
Trained in architecture in Copenhagen, Carlsen immigrated in 1872 to Chicago, shifting his focus to painting. After further study in Paris, he relocated to Boston in 1876, the year he executed this work.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/39691 · CC BY 4.0
